title: Run a Stage 6 Science Fair
overview: Bring together everything from Stage 6 Science to run a science fair that teaches visitors the most important ideas from this stage through real investigations.

project.drivingQuestion: How can we use the science from Stage 6 to run an accurate, safe and exciting science fair for our school or community?
project.finalProduct: Create a science-fair plan with a live investigation, labelled displays, a safety checklist, a visitor survey with a data display, and a short explanation of your scientific decisions.

stages.title: 1. Foundations display
stages.prompt: Choose the two most important ideas from Units 1, 2. Build a display that teaches each idea with a model or diagram, an example and a check question.
stages.evidence: Two labelled displays with models, examples and check questions

stages.title: 2. Live investigation
stages.prompt: Pick one investigation from Units 3, 4 and run it live: state your hypothesis, follow the method, record results and explain your conclusion.
stages.evidence: A completed investigation with hypothesis, method, results and conclusion

stages.title: 3. Connections wall
stages.prompt: Create a connections wall that links ideas from Units 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 to everyday life, with at least three labelled connections.
stages.evidence: A connections wall with three labelled links to daily life

stages.title: 4. Present and explain
stages.prompt: Present your science fair. Explain at least three scientific choices, check that your conclusions match your evidence and identify one improvement you would make.
stages.evidence: Spoken, written or recorded scientific explanation

evidenceChecklist: A safety checklist for every activity
A connections wall with three links
A survey with organised data display

rubric.secure: Observations, measurements, models and conclusions are accurate and checked.
Hypotheses, fair testing, recording and conclusions follow the scientific method.
Labels, diagrams, tables or charts make the science visible.
Decisions are explained using appropriate science words and evidence.

questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.hint: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: heart The heart is the muscular pump; the lungs handle air, not pumping blood.
questions.unitTitle: Humans and Animals: Your Amazing Body Systems

questions.question: During exercise, your heart rate:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: goes up Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster.
questions.unitTitle: Humans and Animals: Your Amazing Body Systems

questions.question: A normal resting heart rate for a child is about:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: 70 to 100 bpm This is the normal resting range for a child.
questions.unitTitle: Humans and Animals: Your Amazing Body Systems

questions.question: In a food chain, the arrow points:
options: from the eater to the food
from the food to the eater
questions.answer: from the food to the eater
questions.hint: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: from the food to the eater. The arrow shows the direction energy flows, into the animal that eats.

questions.question: About how much energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next?
questions.hint: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: 10 percent. About ninety percent is lost as heat and through living and moving, so only about ten percent passes on.

questions.question: The camel's hump, storing fat for the dry season, is an example of a:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: adaptation. Storing fat in the hump is a feature that helps the camel survive dry seasons.

questions.question: Which of these is a reversible change?
questions.hint: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: Melting ghee. Melting only changes the state; the ghee can be cooled back to solid, so it is reversible. The others all make new materials.

questions.question: In salt water, the water is the:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: Solvent. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving — here, the water.

questions.question: Which is a pure substance?
questions.hint: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: Clean water. Pure water is made of only one kind of material. Seawater, air, and rice with stones are all mixtures.

questions.question: A force is best described as:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: A force is a push or a pull. It is neither a colour, a metal, nor a kind of light.

questions.question: A 4 kg object on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) has a weight of:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: Weight = mass x gravity = 4 x 10 = 40 N.

questions.question: When forces on an object are unbalanced, the object will:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 4 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: Unbalanced forces always change an object's motion.

questions.question: Which material is the best electrical conductor?
questions.hint: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: copper — copper is a metal with many free electrons, an excellent conductor used for wires.

questions.question: Adding a second cell in series to a single-bulb circuit will usually make the bulb:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: brighter — a second cell adds voltage (push), driving more current.

questions.question: For safe experiments you should use:
questions.hint: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
questions.explanation: a 1.5 V battery — small batteries are safe; mains and engines are dangerous.

questions.question: Igneous rock forms when:
options: heat and pressure change a rock
questions.hint: The name comes from the Latin for fire.
questions.explanation: Igneous rock forms from molten rock - slowly underground makes large crystals, quickly at the surface makes small ones.
questions.unitTitle: Rocks, Soils and the Rock Cycle

questions.question: Fossils are almost never found in igneous rock because:
options: the rock was molten, so nothing living survived
questions.answer: the rock was molten, so nothing living survived
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a bone at melting temperature.
questions.explanation: Igneous rock formed from molten rock, and nothing living survives that. Fossils need the gentle burying that makes sedimentary rock.
questions.unitTitle: Rocks, Soils and the Rock Cycle

questions.question: In a soil jar test left for a day, the bands from the bottom up are:
questions.hint: The heaviest grains reach the bottom first.
questions.explanation: The largest and heaviest grains settle first, so sand is at the bottom and the finest clay is on top - with organic matter floating above.
questions.unitTitle: Rocks, Soils and the Rock Cycle

questions.question: The Sun is:
questions.hint: It is the only thing in the Solar System making its own light.
questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star. It looks special only because it is so much closer than all the others.

questions.question: Day and night are caused by:
options: the Earth spinning on its axis
the Sun going round the Earth
the Earth's orbit of the Sun
questions.answer: the Earth spinning on its axis
questions.hint: Which motion takes 24 hours?
questions.explanation: The Earth turns once in 24 hours, so every place passes through the lit side and the dark side. The Sun does not move across the sky; we rotate past it.

questions.question: Why can the phases NOT be the Earth's shadow on the Moon?
options: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
the Moon is too far away
the Moon makes its own light
questions.answer: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
questions.hint: Compare how often phases happen with how often eclipses do.
questions.explanation: A shadow needs an exact line-up, which is an eclipse and happens a few times a year. Phases run their full cycle every month, so they must have another cause - our changing view.

questions.question: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence is:
options: equal to the angle of reflection
questions.answer: equal to the angle of reflection
questions.hint: It is the shortest law in this unit.
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.question: A ray strikes a mirror at 35 degrees to the normal. It leaves at:
questions.hint: Apply the law directly.
questions.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so 35 in gives 35 out, on the other side of the normal.

questions.question: A ray passes into a glass block without bending. That means it arrived:
questions.hint: What has to happen for one side of the beam to slow first?
questions.explanation: Arriving square to the surface, the whole beam enters at once, so nothing slows before anything else and there is nothing to pivot the ray.

questions.question: Sperm cells are made in the:
questions.hint: They are held outside the body, in the scrotum.
questions.explanation: The testes make sperm cells, and they begin doing so during puberty.

questions.question: Puberty usually begins between about:
questions.hint: It is a wide range, not a single age.
questions.explanation: The usual range is about 8 to 14, roughly a year or two earlier in girls. Everywhere in that range is normal.

questions.question: Fertilisation is:
options: a sperm cell joining an egg cell
questions.answer: a sperm cell joining an egg cell
questions.hint: You met the same word in the plant units.
questions.explanation: Fertilisation is the joining of the two sex cells, and it is the same idea as pollen joining an ovule in a flowering plant.
